query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating ultrafast scanning calorimetry with in-situ neutron imaging and CALPHAD-guided analysis provides an accurate and efficient route for determining the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and associated volume change of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) across diverse compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized, single-phase high-entropy alloys (e.g., FCC or BCC solid solutions) with high configurational disorder.
generation.intervention: Subject HEA samples to rapid heating using ultrafast differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) while simultaneously recording real-time microstructural evolution via neutron imaging. Coupled analysis with CALPHAD modeling then extracts liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert or vacuum atmosphere over a temperature range spanning from below the melting point to well above it, using high heating rates to suppress kinetic delays.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of a liquid–solid interface during fusion, observable as distinct changes in neutron attenuation profiles and DSC heat flow peaks.
generation.mechanism: Rapid heating minimizes non-equilibrium effects and phase segregation, while in-situ neutron imaging enables direct correlation between calorimetric signals and structural changes. CALPHAD-based models further refine the extraction of enthalpy and entropy of fusion by providing theoretical baselines for phase behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion enthalpy, entropy, melting temperature, and volume change values determined by the combined method will align within ±5–10% of CALPHAD predictions. Moreover, the technique should reveal systematic variations as a function of alloy composition within the HEA family.
generation.baseline: Standard DSC or ex-situ thermal analysis methods that do not account for rapid structural evolution or kinetic effects, often resulting in less accurate thermodynamic parameter estimates.
generation.boundary: Applicability may be limited to HEAs exhibiting relatively simple single-phase behavior prior to melting; alloys with strong multiphase or metastable microstructures might require additional analytical corrections.
generation.uncertainty: The effects of kinetic undercooling and potential phase segregation during rapid heating remain partly uncertain. Calibration may be needed for refractory HEAs or those with complex melting behavior to ensure universal accuracy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA samples with systematically varied compositions. Perform simultaneous ultrafast DSC and in-situ neutron imaging under controlled atmospheric conditions. Compare the obtained thermodynamic parameters with those derived from conventional equilibrium calorimetry and independent CALPHAD predictions.
measurements: DSC heat flow curves and onset/peak temperatures of melting
Neutron imaging data capturing real-time evolution of the melting front and volume changes
Derived enthalpy and entropy of fusion
CALPHAD model outputs for corresponding compositions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated methodology produces melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, entropies, or volume change estimates deviating by more than ±15% relative to conventional measurements and CALPHAD predictions, or if the in-situ imaging does not reveal clear structural transitions correlating with DSC data, then the proposed approach is falsified.

Evidence-based recommender system for high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Existing data-driven approaches for exploring high-entropy alloys (HEAs) face three challenges: numerous element-combination candidates, designing appropriate descriptors, and limited and biased existing data. To overcome these issues, here we show the development of an evidence-based material recommender system (ERS) that adopts Dempster–Shafer theory, a general framework for reasoning with uncertainty. Herein, without using material descriptors, we model, collect and combine pieces of evidence from data about the HEA phase existence of alloys. To evaluate the ERS, we compared its HEA-recommendation capability with those of matrix-factorization- and supervised-learning-based recommender systems on four widely known datasets of up-to-five-component alloys. The k-fold cross-validation on the datasets suggests that the ERS outperforms all competitors. Furthermore, the ERS shows good extrapolation capabilities in recommending quaternary and quinary HEAs. Tunable magnetocaloric effect in transition metal alloys

Abstract: The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. Database on the mechanical properties of high entropy alloys and complex concentrated alloys

Abstract: This data article presents the compilation of mechanical properties for 370 high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) reported in the period from 2004 to 2016. The data sheet includes alloy composition, type of microstructures, density, hardness, type of tests to measure the room temperature mechanical properties, yield strength, elongation, ultimate strength and Young׳s modulus. For 27 refractory HEAs (RHEAs), the yield stress and elongation are given as a function of the testing temperature. The data are stored in a database provided in Supplementary materials, and for practical use they are tabulated in the present paper. The database was used in recent publications by Miracle and Senkov [1], Gorsse et al. [2] and Senkov et al. [3].

Thermal Analysis of High Entropy Rare Earth Oxides

Abstract: AbstractPhase transformations in multicomponent rare earth sesquioxides were studied by splat quenching from the melt, high temperature differential thermal analysis and synchrotron X-ray diffraction on laser-heated samples. Three compositions were prepared by the solution combustion method: (La,Sm,Dy,Er,RE)2O3, where all oxides are in equimolar ratios and RE is Nd or Gd or Y. After annealing at 800 °C, all powders contained mainly a phase of C-type bixbyite structure. After laser melting, all samples were quenched in a single-phase monoclinic B-type structure. Thermal analysis indicated three reversible phase transitions in the range 1900–2400 °C, assigned as transformations into A, H, and X rare earth sesquioxides structure types. Unit cell volumes and volume changes on C-B, B-A, and H-X transformations were measured by X-ray diffraction and consistent with the trend in pure rare earth sesquioxides. The formation of single-phase solid solutions was predicted by Calphad calculations.
